title: Model Overview
text: Predicting Airline Satisfaction — Model Overview. Training set: 699,635 passenger records. Test set: 299,844 records. Model: Logistic Regression (L2 penalty, C=1.0, lbfgs solver). Evaluation: 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Model A (predictive) AUC: 0.9423 with 95% confidence interval [0.9417, 0.9429]. Model B (interpretive) AUC: 0.9228. Brier score: 0.0826. Average precision: 0.9228. Baseline satisfaction rate: 44.4% (mild imbalance, ratio 1.25). Public leaderboard score: 0.94191.

title: Methodology
text: Two logistic regression models were trained. Model A includes all raw service ratings (33 features) and is used for prediction, achieving AUC 0.9423. Model B excludes raw ratings and uses only aggregate features (20 features) including service mean, service min, and service std, achieving AUC 0.9228. Model B exists because survey ratings exhibit a strong halo effect — passengers rate all service dimensions correlatedly — which creates irreducible multicollinearity in any model with all raw ratings. Model B's design matrix is full rank (20/20), so coefficients are uniquely identified with valid confidence intervals and p-values. Rating zeros (survey skips) were replaced with neutral rating 3, with a separate '_not_rated' indicator flag created for each column. Delay features were bucketed into 5 tiers (none, short, medium, long, extreme) and raw minutes were dropped to prevent collinearity. Rare indicator flags (prevalence less than 2%) were pruned. Confidence intervals computed via bootstrap resampling (300 iterations). Coefficient inference uses maximum-likelihood logit on a 150,000-row subsample.

title: What-If Business Lever Analysis
text:
Business lever prioritization via what-if simulation. Each row shows the model-predicted change in average satisfaction probability if that lever improves by +1 rating across all passengers:
  • Online Boarding: lift +4.99 percentage points, cost low, timeline 6 months, priority score 4.99
  • On-Board Service: lift +1.56 percentage points, cost low, timeline 3 months, priority score 3.12
  • Cleanliness: lift +1.00 percentage points, cost low, timeline 2 months, priority score 3.01
  • Checkin Service: lift +1.63 percentage points, cost low, timeline 4 months, priority score 2.44
  • Inflight Wifi Service: lift +5.37 percentage points, cost high, timeline 9 months, priority score 1.19
  • Ease Of Online Booking: lift +0.99 percentage points, cost low, timeline 5 months, priority score 1.19
  • Baggage Handling: lift +0.88 percentage points, cost medium, timeline 6 months, priority score 0.44
  • Inflight Entertainment: lift +0.35 percentage points, cost high, timeline 18 months, priority score 0.04
  • Leg Room Service: lift +0.87 percentage points, cost very_high, timeline 36 months, priority score 0.04
  • Seat Comfort: lift +0.15 percentage points, cost very_high, timeline 36 months, priority score 0.01
Priority score = lift_pp / (cost_weight × time_weight). Highest priority score is Online boarding (+5.02 pp, low cost, 6 months, score 5.02). The Food and Drink lever was excluded because its what-if estimate was negative — a statistical artifact of collinearity, not a real signal.

title: Priority Recommendations
text: Recommended priority actions (model-predicted associations, not causal effects): P1 — Online Boarding: +5.0 percentage-point predicted lift, low cost, 6-month timeline. The single best investment under the priority heuristic. P1 — On-Board Service: +1.6 pp lift, low cost, 3-month timeline. P2 — Cleanliness: +1.0 pp, low cost, 2-month timeline. P2 — Check-in Service: +1.6 pp, low cost, 4-month timeline. P2 — WiFi Upgrade: highest absolute lift (+5.4 pp) but high cost and 9-month horizon. P3 — Inflight entertainment, leg room, seat comfort: capital-intensive retrofits, defer.

title: Limitations & Caveats
text: Critical caveats for interpreting this model's outputs: This analysis identifies STATISTICAL ASSOCIATIONS, NOT CAUSAL EFFECTS. All lift estimates are model-predicted changes in probability, not field outcomes. A controlled pilot is required to establish whether improving a lever actually causes satisfaction to rise. Financial ROI cannot be computed without revenue-per-passenger and cost-of-implementation data, which are not present in this dataset. The priority score is a ranking heuristic, not a financial return. There is a halo effect in survey ratings — passengers rate service dimensions correlatedly — which means individual touchpoint contributions cannot be cleanly separated. service_std (rating variance) has a positive coefficient that is counterintuitive; possible interpretations are respondent engagement or a selection artifact. The dataset appears synthetically generated; real-world effect sizes may differ.

Key Findings
1. Segment dominates satisfaction. Type of Travel and Customer Type are the two strongest predictors —
together carrying more signal than any individual service touchpoint.
2. Online boarding is the highest-leverage service lever. A +1-rating improvement is associated with a
+5.0 percentage-point increase in predicted satisfaction probability — at low cost and a 6-month timeline.
3. WiFi quality is the largest absolute lever. +5.4 pp predicted lift, but high cost and 9-month horizon push
it to P3 on the priority heuristic.
4. Consistency of experience ranks #5 in SHAP importance. Passengers with varied ratings tend to be
more satisfied than those who rate uniformly — but this likely reflects respondent engagement rather than a
causal lever.
5. Demographics (age, gender) do not materially drive satisfaction. Once segment and service are
accounted for, age and gender have near-zero, statistically non-significant effects.

title: Report — Page 9
text:
Airline Satisfaction Report · Page 9
5.1 Odds Ratios & Interpretation
 Figure 6: Odds ratios with 95% CIs.
Reading the Coefficients
  service_mean (OR ≈ 4.46): A 1-SD increase in avg service rating multiplies satisfaction odds by ~4.5×.
 Type of Travel (OR ≈ 3.53): Business-travel passengers have ~3.5× higher odds.
 Customer Type (OR ≈ 2.20): Loyal customers have ~2.2× higher odds.
 service_std (OR ≈ 1.96): Higher rating variance correlates with higher satisfaction — see caveat.
 Class (OR ≈ 1.57): Each step up in cabin class multiplies odds by ~1.57×.
 delay_medium (OR ≈ 0.91): 16–60 min delays reduce odds by ~9%.
Note on the service_std direction
A positive coefficient on rating variance is counterintuitive. Two interpretations exist:
 Engagement: Passengers who rate with variation are opinionated and engaged.
 Selection artifact: May reflect a demographic or segment confound.
We cannot distinguish without controlled data. Do not treat “increase rating variance” as an actionable lever.

title: Report — Page 15
text:
Airline Satisfaction Report · Page 15
9. Limitations & Caveats
 What this model CAN tell you
 Which service touchpoints are most associated with passenger satisfaction.
 How much predicted satisfaction probability changes if a touchpoint improves.
 Which passenger segments have systematically different satisfaction profiles.
What this model CANNOT tell you
 Causality. All effects are observational. A controlled pilot is required to establish causal effect.
 Financial ROI. Revenue per passenger, upgrade cost, churn elasticity are not in the data.
 Field-effect magnitude. Lift estimates are model-implied and may not translate one-to-one.
 Behavioral intent. Survey answers are self-reported.
Additional Caveats
  Halo effect in ratings. Passengers rate service dimensions correlatedly. Model A keeps all ratings for
prediction; only Model B's aggregate coefficients are statistically valid for inference.
 Synthetic dataset. Appears synthetically generated based on real airline survey structure. Real-world
effect sizes may differ.
 service_std direction. The positive coefficient on rating variance is interpreted as engagement, but this
is one of several possible readings.
 What-if reliability. Model A's predictions are accurate within the observed feature distribution but less
reliable for out-of-distribution simulations.
